claims.statement: deepagents-code (dcode) is a prebuilt terminal coding agent that packages the deepagents SDK harness together with a terminal experience, persistence, tools, skills, and optional sandboxed execution, as a reference implementation.

dcode has two runtime halves that run in separate processes: a terminal client that owns presentation and input (interactive or headless output plus approvals), and an agent server that owns the agent runtime and connects the model, tools, memory, skills, and backend.

`DeepAgentsApp` composes the startup tip, goal-status panel, chat input, and docked status bar; after first paint it constructs the Textual adapter with callbacks for rendering, approvals, status, accounting, skills, and Auto-mode events before starting background initialization.

The two-line status bar keeps hook and agent messages in separate slots so hooks override only while nonempty, uses plain `Content` for hook-configured text, and shares one spinner between connection and busy indications that is stopped on unmount.

`ServerConfig` is the shared client-to-server configuration schema: the launcher writes its serialized `DEEPAGENTS_CODE_SERVER_*` mapping and the server reconstructs it with `from_env`; relative paths are normalized before serialization because the subprocess has a different working directory.

The server, not the client, authorizes project-scoped workspace policy: it rejects claimed project fields, verifies the client-claimable session policy fingerprint, resolves policy for the canonical target directory, and persists the server-authoritative workspace payload with the thread binding.

Changing workspace directories fails closed for project execution policy: dcode drops launch-project MCP configuration, sandbox setup, and extension paths, then re-reads extension trust for the target project instead of applying one checkout's policy to another.

The CLI dispatches `-n` to one headless task and otherwise launches the Textual app; headless mode runs a server session with `interactive=False`, streams the remote agent through a console loop, and its shell policy defaults to disabled unless a shell allow-list is configured.

The server constructs a runtime by snapshotting workspace environment and credentials, configuring tracing, resolving a model and tools, optionally opening a sandbox, and compiling the CLI agent; the resulting runtime contains the graph, composite backend, server-owned offload operation, and metadata.

For a request with execution context, the graph factory requires a thread ID and workspace context, validates the thread binding, and selects a workspace runtime; bound policy drift is rejected, while a runtime-fingerprint-only change rebuilds the runtime without invalidating the binding.

Server shutdown is ownership-aware: `server_session` cleans MCP sessions and stops the child in a finally block, `ServerProcess.stop()` is idempotent and concurrency-safe, and POSIX teardown signals the detached server process group with SIGTERM before SIGKILL escalation.
Headless teardown drains pending hook work and releases a held thread lease, so asynchronous hook dispatch and thread ownership do not outlive the one-task process.

The server launcher builds a temporary `langgraph dev` workspace, starts it on an ephemeral local port, waits for the `agent` graph, and configures the returned `RemoteAgent` with an explicit workspace and client-claimable session-policy fingerprint; failures before handoff stop the child.

`RemoteAgent` lazily creates a `RemoteGraph`, binds or retrieves a server-validated workspace per thread, and injects that workspace payload into streamed graph context; it fails rather than issuing a workspace-dependent request without configured workspace state.

ACP mode is an in-process stdio execution surface: it opens a persistent checkpointer, builds an agent per ACP session, fences sessions with thread leases, and cleans MCP sessions and remaining leases when the server exits.

When ACP Auto mode is active, dcode wraps the ACP server to store trusted Auto approval state and attaches prompt metadata to the user message before graph streaming; the wrapper delegates state operations to the underlying graph.

The server runtime factory caches construction under a lock because repeated MCP discovery, sandbox creation, and atexit registration would leak or duplicate process-lifetime resources; the graph and offload API share that runtime.
`ServerConfig` enforces that a shell allow-list is either absent or nonempty and that an explicit filesystem tool allowlist is nonempty and includes `read_file`.

The launcher scaffolds a generated runtime with a persistent SQLite checkpointer whose database path is supplied through the server environment, and the generated LangGraph configuration registers the built-in agent graph plus dcode's custom authenticated HTTP application.

Server startup uses a separate graph-readiness request after health polling so lazy graph-construction failures surface before handoff; cancellation or failure during startup reaps the child, using shortened grace only when no sandbox is configured.

Windows server shutdown uses a new console process group and Ctrl+Break with terminate fallback, but hard escalation kills only the root process, unlike POSIX process-group escalation which can kill descendants.

A remote agent's cost tracker retains main-task and side-question subtotals independently, rejects stale lower main-task totals, and combines them only for presentation so delayed data cannot erase already observed spend.

The sessions database stores LangGraph checkpoint persistence and supports cached thread metadata derived from checkpoint freshness; a remote thread's live HTTP record can be idempotently recreated after a server restart even when checkpoint state remains on disk.

The client puts the server-validated workspace descriptor in each remote graph stream context, and the server requires that context to match the durable thread binding before selecting a workspace runtime.

The generated checkpointer installs an idempotent compatibility patch that forwards delta-channel history reads through the LangGraph custom adapter to an inner saver only when that saver overrides the base method, retaining the base walk otherwise.

Server tracing is pinned for the process lifetime: workspaces with different LangSmith tracing settings are refused, and the server installs an override that runs only untraced traceable setup/end bookkeeping inline while preserving the standard thread hop for other calls.

During its HTTP lifespan, dcode conditionally patches the in-memory LangGraph run queue so a completed `Runs.put` wakes a waiting `Runs.next`; the stock claim operation, queue order, and thread locking remain intact, with a shape-checked no-op fallback and a 0.5-second timeout.

Interactive startup can prespawn the server before the app module loads, holds readiness until adoption after the app paint gate, and cancels or reaps an unadopted start rather than leaving its child process behind.

On POSIX, the server bootstrap watches a parent-owned pipe and terminates the server with a graceful signal followed by SIGKILL after the shutdown timeout when the client disappears, including if normal interpreter teardown stalls.
